scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] Meet the Glessner House.

[short pause] It is a summer morning in 1904, at 1800 Prairie Avenue. The morning sun shines off the lake onto the stone front. John Glessner lives here. He sells farm machines and comes from Ohio. [short pause] His wife, Frances, has kept a diary since 1879. [short pause] And here is the house that shocked the street.

[short pause] There are ten stops on foot, all the way around one house. You will see the corner, the side street, the alley, the front door, the carriage tunnel and the courtyard inside. Most of the story comes from Mr. Glessner. [short pause] He wrote it down for his children in 1923. [short pause] You will only see the outside.

[short pause] Start at the corner, where the neighbors first saw the house and did not like it.
scripts.stop:corner: [wistfully] People used to call Prairie Avenue the sunny street for the chosen few. [short pause] Pullman's mansion stands across the corner. Kimball's French castle is across the street. Then there is this one, with rough stone, small deep windows and steep red roofs. It was the last house Henry Richardson designed. [short pause] He never saw it built.
scripts.stop:north-wall: [curious] People talked about this side when the house was new. [short pause] They noticed the narrow windows, just big enough to light the halls. Richardson said city windows were not for looking out of. People just cover them with shades and curtains anyway. [short pause] So the house keeps its back to the street.
scripts.stop:arch: [measured] The great arch is the back door. [short pause] A small hall through it leads to the kitchen. It is also how music sneaks in. On New Year's Day 1903, eight horn players slipped in by this door. [short pause] They went up the back stairs, and at four o'clock they began to play in the upstairs hall.
scripts.stop:stable: [measured] The west side is the stable and carriage house. [short pause] Its wide carriage door opens onto Eighteenth Street. Inside, the walls are white shiny brick. The furnace room is under the stable. [short pause] That way the dust, dirt and noise of coal and ashes never come into the house.
scripts.stop:gate: [measured] Around the corner, these gates in the alley open into the courtyard. [short pause] The Glessners used them for a trick. On 1 December 1887 the family moved everything in through here before the neighbors even guessed they were moving. [short pause] That night they lit the new fireplace with fire carried from the old house.
scripts.stop:door: [measured] This is the front door. [short pause] It is heavy oak with iron straps and a small window behind an iron grille. Richardson would not let anyone paint the iron. It was treated a special way so it would not rust. [short pause] The wall looks like solid rock, but it is really brick covered with big granite slabs.
scripts.stop:porte: [playfully] Not every visitor uses the front door. [short pause] Here a carriage could leave Prairie Avenue and roll right under the house. It went through two big oak doors hung on heavy iron straps, and out into a private courtyard. [short pause] Follow it through.
scripts.stop:court-north: [warmly] Inside, the house changes. [short pause] From the street it looked shut tight. Here it opens up. Richardson put big windows on this sunny courtyard side. Mr. Glessner wrote that they let in a flood of sunlight when the sun shines in Chicago. [short pause] The family rooms look in at this quiet yard, not out at the street.
scripts.stop:hall-bow: [measured] The round part above the steps is the front hall. [short pause] Its door to the courtyard has yellow glass in it, so the hall feels sunny even on grey days. The vines here came from the family's old house. One was fifty-five feet long and was planted again in one piece. [short pause] It grew well.
scripts.stop:family: [warmly] Behind these walls, 1904 is a busy year. [short pause] Frances Glessner has set up a workbench in the basement to make silver things. Every winter and spring her Monday Reading Class meets in the library. [short pause] Years ago her son George and his friends ran a telegraph company from his room, with wires to seven houses.
scripts.ending:finish: [softly] Richardson never saw any of this. He was very sick in April 1886. Three weeks before he died, he marked on the drawings where the lights would go. He told Mr. Glessner that his part was finished. [short pause] Digging began that June, and the Glessner children threw the first shovels of dirt. [short pause] Mr. Glessner believed it was the house Richardson would most have liked to live in himself.
